demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Triggers.value: Physical pain in a part of the body

Threat.value: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me

Memory.value: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
When I remember the event I feel intense rage
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something about me that made the event happen
I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me

vignette:
David had spent thirty years as a forester, a man who understood the predictable physics of falling timber and the quiet language of the woods. At fifty-four, he'd believed he could rely on his own judgment above all else. That conviction ended nine months ago, on a damp Tuesday afternoon. He had been supervising a selective logging crew when he misjudged the lean of an old-growth fir. He saw the shift, the sickeningly slow pivot in the wrong direction, and shouted, but it was too late. The sound, the splintering crack, was forever fused with the image of Leo, the newest member of his crew, disappearing beneath the weight of it.

In the weeks that followed, the forest, once his sanctuary, became a place of ambush. The scent of pine sap or the distant whine of a chainsaw would instantly pull him back to that afternoon, the memory arriving not as a thought but as a full-body seizure. He would feel an excruciating lock in his own back, his muscles contorting into the same strained position he'd held while trying to lift the immense weight from Leo's shattered body. This physical reenactment was always accompanied by a wave of grief so profound it felt like drowning, immediately followed by a hot, useless rage directed squarely at himself. The memory wasn't just a replay; it was evidence. Each time it surfaced, it hammered home the belief that this wasn't an accident but a failing woven into his very character. He simply could not rely on himself.

This sense of being fundamentally flawed began to bleed into every corner of his life. A simple, nagging ache in his shoulder, a somatic echo of the accident, would trigger a cascade of fear. The pain was a reminder of his physical limits, of his failure, and it left him feeling intensely vulnerable, unable to relax even in his own living room. This constant state of threat made him a stranger in his own home; he found himself watching his wife's movements, scanning for signs of... he wasn't even sure what. Out in public, any stranger who approached too quickly sent a spike of panic through him, his mind convinced that harm was imminent, that his faulty judgment would fail to protect him again. This pervasive sense of danger served as its own irrefutable logic; a capable man wouldn't feel this terrified all the time, which only confirmed his growing belief that he was fundamentally and irrevocably broken. Living with this constant hum of danger, he began to find that even benign events could feel like warnings; the groan of a floorboard or a sudden gust of wind against the house now registered as signs of imminent structural collapse, fresh evidence of a world that could betray him at any moment.

The cycles have grown tighter, more vicious, over the months. His hypervigilance now acts as its own kind of bait. While watching other people closely for signs of a threat he cannot define, his tense state of mind will inevitably conjure the memory of the paramedics rushing towards Leo, their faces grim. The memory itself then triggers the familiar, agonizing cramp in his back, a somatic reminder that reinforces his vigilance. This loop is relentless: the feeling of threat summons the memory, the memory brings the physical pain, and the pain amplifies his sense of being under constant threat. It is in these moments that the appraisals feel most true. The image of Leo's still form, triggered by the sight of a stranger on the street, reinforces the devastating thought that there is something intrinsically wrong with him, that he is no longer the capable man who once felt at home in the world.

He was forced to take an extended leave from work. The man whose identity was carved from his competence in the wild was now unable to even walk a wooded trail near his house without being overwhelmed. The proximity to the trees was enough to start the cycle, the appraisal that he was no longer capable of the very things that had defined him becoming a self-fulfilling prophecy. It was after his wife found him frozen in the doorway, unable to step outside for fear of what he might see or feel, that they agreed he needed help. David came to therapy not with a clear hope, but with a desperate question: how can a man learn to trust himself again when his own body and mind provide constant, irrefutable proof that he is broken?

violations.explanation: The vignette does not contain a causal link where a sense of threat leads to or creates new triggers.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Threat → Triggers: The vignette does not contain a causal link where a sense of threat leads to or creates new triggers.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."
